title: AI boom powers fears for grid, push for rule change
full_text:
Australia’s ambitions to become a global artificial intelligence powerhouse have prompted energy regulators to seek a rewrite of the electricity rule book, with giant data centres facing tougher technical standards amid concerns they could pose new risks to the stability of the national grid.
The Australian Energy Market Operator has asked the Australian Energy Market Commission to introduce new rules for large inverter-based electricity users, arguing the rapid growth of AI data centres and other power-hungry industrial facilities is exposing gaps in a regulatory framework developed before such technologies emerged.
The proposal underscores a growing challenge confronting the Albanese government as it courts billions of dollars of investment in AI infrastructure while overseeing the transition to a renewable-powered electricity system. As data centres become some of the country’s biggest electricity users, regulators want to ensure they do not inadvertently undermine the reliability of the grid during faults or other disturbances.
Unlike traditional factories, modern AI data centres are powered through sophisticated electronic equipment known as inverters rather than large spinning motors. While the technology allows facilities to operate more efficiently, it also means they can react almost instantaneously to changes in voltage or frequency on the electricity network.
Energy regulators are increasingly concerned that if several large data centres respond unpredictably or disconnect simultaneously during a disturbance, they could exacerbate instability on the electricity system.
Under the proposed rule change, large inverter-based loads above 30 megawatts would be required to remain connected during short-lived voltage and frequency disturbances, rather than automatically disconnecting. They would also need to meet new technical performance standards governing how they respond during faults and provide more detailed information to network operators before connecting to the electricity system.
AEMC chair Anna Collyer said the proposed changes were aimed at ensuring the electricity rules kept pace with rapid changes across the energy system.
“Clear grid standards are essential to supporting Australia’s data centre growth without compromising system security,” Ms Collyer said. The AEMC will now consult on the proposed rule.
